screens.title: Getting Started with the Databricks Workspace
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will become confident navigating the Databricks Workspace and performing the basic operations that let you begin real data engineering work. We'll orient you to the left-hand navigation, the Workspace browser for organizing notebooks and folders, and the Data and Compute panes you use every day. You will learn how to create a new notebook, choose a default language, attach it to a cluster, and run simple Spark operations that read data from the Databricks File System. Along the way you'll see how to mix Python and S Q L in the same notebook, why the display command is useful for inspecting results, and how dbutils. fs lets you explore DBFS directories. A common mistake is forgetting to attach a notebook to a running cluster; we'll explain how to avoid that. By the end of this chapter you'll be ready to create a notebook, read a sample CSV from DBFS, transform it with Spark, and run an aggregation with S Q L. Keep an eye out for practical steps and small checks that prevent errors when you work in a shared environment.

screens.title: The Databricks Workspace UI
screens.narratorSegment: The Databricks Workspace UI is the graphical hub where you find notebooks, data, compute, jobs, and integration points. At its core the left-hand sidebar exposes sections like Workspace for organizing notebooks and folders, Recents for quick access, Data for tables and databases, Compute for cluster lifecycle management, Jobs for scheduling, MLflow for model lifecycle, and Repos for Git integration. Each section plays a distinct role: Workspace is your file organization, Compute is where execution happens, and Data surfaces metadata about tables. For a concrete example, imagine you need to run a scheduled job that reads a table, transforms it, and writes a Delta table. You would: locate the code in Workspace or Repos, verify the Data catalog for the table location, attach the notebook to an appropriate cluster from Compute, and create a job to schedule the notebook. A common misconception is that notebooks alone carry compute — they do not. Notebooks must be attached to running clusters to execute Spark code. A practical check is to always verify cluster status and the target table path before running a job. How will you verify the cluster and table before execution?

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Workspace UI
Definition

What the Workspace provides

A unified interface for code, data, compute and lifecycle tools used in data engineering workflows.

Workspace: organize notebooks and folders for collaboration.
Data: browse tables and storage references used in jobs.
Compute: manage clusters that run your notebook code.
Role-based example
Developer
Stores notebooks in Workspace or Repos, tests code on a small cluster, commits to version control.
Data Engineer
Checks Data catalog, attaches to Compute for ETL jobs, schedules with Jobs when ready.
Analyst
Uses notebooks to run queries and visualizations with display for exploration.
ML Practitioner
Uses MLflow and Repos to manage experiments and model code.
Key Takeaway

Treat the sidebar sections as distinct tools. Confirm compute and data references before running production tasks.

screens.title: Creating and organizing notebooks
screens.narratorSegment: Creating and organizing notebooks is a simple process with powerful implications for collaboration. First, when you create a notebook, give it a descriptive name that reflects its purpose and environment, for example 'DBFS_Data_Exploration' for a data inspection task. Choose a sensible default language — Python is common for data engineering — but remember you can mix languages using magic commands. Organize notebooks into folders that reflect projects, teams, or pipeline stages. A clear folder hierarchy reduces friction when teammates search for work. A practical example: create a project folder, create a Python notebook inside it, and add a README or index notebook that lists the purpose of each item. A common misconception is that the default language locks you out of other languages; it doesn't. Use cell-level magic commands like a S Q L magic when you need to run aggregations or a different kernel for quick tests. Before sharing, export or place notebooks in Repos if you require Git history. As a closing question, how will you name and folder structure your first project so others can find it?

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Create & Organize
Steps

Create a notebook and organize it

  1. 1. Open Workspace and choose a project folder or create one.
  2. 2. Click New Notebook, supply a descriptive name and pick a default language.
  3. 3. Attach the notebook to a cluster for execution.
  4. 4. Add a README notebook or folder-level index to document purpose and owners.
Mnemonic: Name, Language, Attach, Document — a short checklist to follow before executing code destined for reuse.
Concrete example
DBFS_Data_Exploration
A Python notebook in /Projects/AutoData that reads sample CSVs and documents data shape and sources.
Common mistake
Using vague names like 'notebook1' — that makes later discovery and ownership difficult.
Key Takeaway

A small investment in naming and structure saves time for the whole team.

screens.title: Attaching notebooks to clusters and executing cells
screens.narratorSegment: Attaching a notebook to a cluster connects your interactive code to compute capable of running Spark workloads. A cluster provides driver and worker processes that execute code and manage Spark's runtime. When you attach, your notebook gains a spark session which is the programmatic entry point to Spark operations. To run a code cell, use the execution shortcut shown in the UI — commonly Shift plus Enter — and inspect outputs beneath the cell. A concrete example: after creating a small test cluster, attach your Python notebook and run a simple display command that renders a DataFrame. If the notebook is not attached, you'll receive an error when trying to run Spark operations. A common misconception is assuming attaching to any cluster is safe; choose a cluster sized for the task and ensure you have the right permissions. Always confirm cluster status and owner, and run an inexpensive sanity cell first, such as printing a small message or listing a DBFS folder. How will you check cluster readiness before running heavy transformations? Attaching notebooks to clusters and executing cells means a notebook must be attached to a running cluster to execute spark commands; verify cluster readiness first.. In practical terms, how compute is connected to notebooks and how to run code safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Cluster Attachment
Architecture

Notebook ↔ Cluster ↔ Spark

Notebooks are UI clients that send code to a cluster. The cluster runs Spark, and results stream back to the notebook for display. The spark session is provided by the cluster process and is required for DataFrame operations.
Sanity check example: run a lightweight cell that prints a message or lists a DBFS folder to confirm connectivity.
Sizing note: pick a test cluster for quick development and a larger cluster for heavier ETL to avoid runaway costs or failures.
Example run
# After attaching to a running cluster
# Create a small DataFrame and display it
sample_df = spark.createDataFrame([(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')], ['id','val'])
display(sample_df)
Common mistake
Trying to run Spark code without confirming the notebook is attached to a running cluster.
Key Takeaway

Always attach and run a lightweight check before heavy transformations to avoid wasted compute and errors.

keyIdea.text: Use Spark read, display for inspection, then create a temporary view for SQL analysis or further transformations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Read CSV
Code Example
# Read a CSV file from DBFS
df = spark.read.format("csv") \
  .option("header", "true") \
  .option("inferSchema", "true") \
  .load("/databricks-datasets/samples/auto/auto-mpg.csv")

# Display the DataFrame
display(df)

# Create a temporary view for SQL
df.createOrReplaceTempView("auto_mpg_data")
This code demonstrates reading from DBFS, rendering an interactive table with display, and registering a temp view so SQL cells can query the DataFrame.
Explanation
  • Option header true instructs Spark to use the first row as column names.
  • Infer schema attempts to detect column types for convenience during exploration.
  • display renders a rich table view with quick visualization options built in.
  • Temporary views let you switch to SQL for aggregation without persisting tables.
Misconception
Relying on inferred schema in production can be brittle; favor explicit schemas for reproducible pipelines.
Key Takeaway

Read, inspect, and then register a temp view when you want to combine Python and SQL exploration steps.

screens.title: Mixing languages: magic commands
screens.narratorSegment: Databricks notebooks let you choose a default language for convenience, but you can run code in other languages within individual cells using magic commands. The typical magic for S Q L is the percent sql command at the top of a cell. For example, after creating a temporary view from a DataFrame, you can run an aggregation in a S Q L cell to compute averages by grouping. This mixing is powerful because it lets you use Python for data ingestion and transformations, then use S Q L for concise aggregations and joins when that is more readable. A concrete contrast: instead of rewriting an aggregation using the DataFrame A P I, the S Q L magic gives direct, declarative aggregation syntax. A common misconception is thinking magic commands change the notebook-level language; they only change the interpreter for that single cell. As a practical check, create a temp view in Python, then run a S Q L magic cell to compute an average and verify results match a Python aggregation. Which form will be clearer for your team: S Q L or DataFrame APIs?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Magic Commands
Comparison

SQL magic vs DataFrame API

SQL magic
Concise, declarative queries for aggregations and joins. Ideal for analysts and quick grouping tasks.
DataFrame API
Programmatic transformations and complex logic in Python or Scala. Better for reusable functions and custom UDFs.
Example
%sql
SELECT origin, COUNT(*) FROM auto_mpg_data GROUP BY origin;
This SQL magic cell runs against the temporary view created from the DataFrame. Results appear as a table in the notebook output, just like display from Python.
Misconception
Magic commands do not change the notebook default; they only change the interpreter for the current cell.
Key Takeaway

Use the language that makes the operation clearer; mix cell-level magic for the best readability and productivity.

screens.title: Databricks File System (DBFS)
screens.narratorSegment: DBFS is a distributed file system mounted into the Databricks Workspace and made available on clusters. It is an abstraction over cloud object storage like ADLS Gen2 or S3 and provides paths your notebooks can read from and write to. You interact with DBFS using the dbutils. fs utility, which provides commands to list directories, read files, and write or remove items. For example, dbutils. fs. ls lists contents of a path and is a safe first check before deeper operations. A concrete example: listing the sample datasets directory and then opening a specific CSV file to inspect its schema helps prevent path errors. A common and serious mistake is running a removal command without verifying the target path; dbutils. fs. rm can permanently delete files if used without care. Best practice is to list and preview before delete, and to keep backups or use version control for important assets. After exploring DBFS, ask yourself: have you confirmed the exact path and contents before modifying or deleting files? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › DBFS & dbutils
Definition & Commands
DBFS provides a convenient mounted namespace for storage. Use dbutils.fs to inspect and manage files; treat DBFS paths like file system locations but remember they map to cloud object storage.
# List a directory and a specific dataset folder
print("Contents of /databricks-datasets:")
dbutils.fs.ls("/databricks-datasets")

print("Contents of /databricks-datasets/samples/auto:")
dbutils.fs.ls("/databricks-datasets/samples/auto/")
Safety notes
Always list and preview before modifying or deleting files.
dbutils.fs.rm can remove files; confirm the target path to avoid accidental loss.
Use export or backup for important notebooks and assets before destructive actions.
Common mistake
Running delete commands without confirming the path or contents first, leading to irreversible deletion.
Key Takeaway

Treat DBFS like any shared storage: inspect, confirm, and back up before destructive operations.

screens.title: Common notebook operations: save, export, import, and Repos
screens.narratorSegment: Notebooks in Databricks save automatically, but you still need to manage exports, imports, and versioning thoughtfully. You can export notebooks in formats like notebook archives or Jupyter formats to share outside Databricks. Import lets you bring notebooks from other environments or backups into your Workspace. For team-based development, Repos integrates with Git providers so you can track changes and collaborate in a familiar workflow. A practical flow: commit local changes to a Git branch via Repos for peer review, and export an archive if you need to provide a portable snapshot. One misconception is assuming auto-save replaces version control; auto-save preserves recent edits but does not give the same history or branching capabilities as Git. Use exports for ad-hoc sharing and Repos for ongoing collaboration. Before exporting, strip sensitive credentials and check that printed outputs do not contain secrets. How will you combine Repos and exports to share reproducible work safely? screens.title: Common errors and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring issues can slow you down when working in Databricks. First, attaching a notebook to an incorrect or inactive cluster is the most common cause of runtime errors. Always verify cluster status and owner to ensure you have appropriate compute and permissions. Second, path mistakes on DBFS are frequent: a missing slash, wrong folder name, or mistaken case leads to file not found errors. Use dbutils. fs. ls to confirm the exact path before loading data. Third, implicit schema inference can yield unexpected types; check the DataFrame schema early and prefer explicit schemas for production pipelines. Fourth, sharing notebooks without removing credentials, tokens, or connection strings exposes secrets — always scrub notebooks before export or commit. A practical action is to adopt a short pre-run checklist: verify attachment, list paths, preview a small sample, and confirm that no secrets are present. After this checklist, you can run the full job with higher confidence. Welcome. In this lesson you will become confident navigating the Databricks Workspace and performing the basic operations that let you begin real data engineering work. We'll orient you to the left-hand navigation, the Workspace browser for organizing notebooks and folders, and the Data and Compute panes you use every day. You will learn how to create a new notebook, choose a default language, attach it to a cluster, and run simple Spark operations that read data from the Databricks File System. Along the way you'll see how to mix Python and S Q L in the same notebook, why the display command is useful for inspecting results, and how dbutils. fs lets you explore DBFS directories. A common mistake is forgetting to attach a notebook to a running cluster; we'll explain how to avoid that. By the end of this chapter you'll be ready to create a notebook, read a sample CSV from DBFS, transform it with Spark, and run an aggregation with S Q L. Keep an eye out for practical steps and small checks that prevent errors when you work in a shared environment.

These objectives will guide your practice in the workspace. First, you will be able to navigate the key sections of the Databricks UI — the Workspace browser, Data, Compute, Jobs, Repos, and MLflow — and explain why each section matters for collaboration and pipeline development. Second, you will create, organize, and manage notebooks and folders, choosing default languages and using magic commands to combine Python, S Q L, Scala, and R when needed. Third, you will attach a notebook to a cluster and run basic Spark operations, using commands that read a CSV from DBFS and render results. Fourth, you will understand DBFS as a mounted abstraction over cloud object storage and use dbutils. fs to list, read, and write files safely. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or mental check so you remember to verify your cluster connection, language mode, and file paths before running heavy jobs. These abilities prepare you to move beyond exploration to reliable, repeatable data tasks and safe collaboration with colleagues.

These objectives emphasize practical habits and safety. First, adopt a simple naming convention and folder hierarchy so teammates can find and reuse notebooks. Third, practice safe DBFS operations: use list and preview commands before writing or deleting files. Fourth, learn to export and import notebooks to share work or move it between environments, and understand the role of Repos for Git-backed version control. Each objective includes a competence check: can you create a notebook, attach it to a cluster, read a file from DBFS, and export the notebook as an archive? These habits reduce accidental data loss, ensure reproducibility, and make collaboration more reliable when multiple engineers use the same workspace.

The Databricks Workspace UI is the graphical hub where you find notebooks, data, compute, jobs, and integration points. At its core the left-hand sidebar exposes sections like Workspace for organizing notebooks and folders, Recents for quick access, Data for tables and databases, Compute for cluster lifecycle management, Jobs for scheduling, MLflow for model lifecycle, and Repos for Git integration. Each section plays a distinct role: Workspace is your file organization, Compute is where execution happens, and Data surfaces metadata about tables. For a concrete example, imagine you need to run a scheduled job that reads a table, transforms it, and writes a Delta table. You would: locate the code in Workspace or Repos, verify the Data catalog for the table location, attach the notebook to an appropriate cluster from Compute, and create a job to schedule the notebook. A common misconception is that notebooks alone carry compute — they do not. Notebooks must be attached to running clusters to execute Spark code. Creating and organizing notebooks is a simple process with powerful implications for collaboration. Attaching a notebook to a cluster connects your interactive code to compute capable of running Spark workloads. A cluster provides driver and worker processes that execute code and manage Spark's runtime. When you attach, your notebook gains a spark session which is the programmatic entry point to Spark operations. To run a code cell, use the execution shortcut shown in the UI — commonly Shift plus Enter — and inspect outputs beneath the cell. A concrete example: after creating a small test cluster, attach your Python notebook and run a simple display command that renders a DataFrame. Second, path mistakes on DBFS are frequent: a missing slash, wrong folder name, or mistaken case leads to file not found errors. Use dbutils. fs. ls to confirm the exact path before loading data. Third, implicit schema inference can yield unexpected types; check the DataFrame schema early and prefer explicit schemas for production pipelines. Fourth, sharing notebooks without removing credentials, tokens, or connection strings exposes secrets — always scrub notebooks before export or commit. A practical action is to adopt a short pre-run checklist: verify attachment, list paths, preview a small sample, and confirm that no secrets are present. After this checklist, you can run the full job with higher confidence.
